BP are effective in reducing the risk of skeletal-related events (SREs) and are safe in patients with bone disease from solid tumours, with the exception of osteonecrosis of the jaw.
BP are effective and safe in patients with bone cancer metastases and in patients who are at risk of developing bone cancer metastases.
BP should be used in metastatic bone disease, and for patients at risk of CTIBL.

developing a new class of drugs, which are called bisphosphonate derivatives, for the treatment of osteoporosis.
the use of BP for prevention of skeletal events in patients with bone-metastatic breast cancer.
the development of new, more effective drugs for the treatment of bone metastasis and osteolytic bone diseases, as well as with the improvement of the existing drugs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

all BP are effective in reducing the incidence of skeletal complications, but that the optimal dose, schedule and route of administration are still being investigated and may differ according to the specific cancer type.
the use of BP is recommended as supportive therapy in patients with bone disease, and that the use of ZOL is recommended for patients with bone metastasis from solid tumours.

the use of BP for prevention or treatment of CTIBL and for prevention of bone metastases in high-risk patients is supported by evidence, and that their use for the treatment of bone metastases from breast cancer is supported by high-level evidence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of BP is safe and efficacious in the treatment of bone metastasis, but the choice of the specific agent depends on several factors, including the type of tumour, the stage of the disease, and the individual patient.
BP are effective, well tolerated, and safe in the treatment of cancer patients with bone metastasis, and may be considered for prevention of CTIBL.

BP are a well-established class of drugs for the prevention and treatment of cancer-related bone diseases, and that their efficacy and safety have been demonstrated in several clinical trials and in daily clinical practice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a strong evidence basis for the use of BP as adjuvant therapy in early breast cancer patients to prevent CTIBL, and the panel strongly recommends their use for this indication.

BP are effective in reducing the risk of skeletal-related events (SREs) in breast cancer and in patients with bone lesions due to prostate cancer, lung cancer, renal cancer and other solid tumours, and should be considered as part of the treatment plan.
